subject: hoverPickup
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: militarized pickup converted to hover thrusters.
Style: low-poly cyberpunk.
reasoning:
I'm planning a self-contained TypeScript module for a low-poly cyberpunk hover-pickup, aiming for a rich part count with textures, paint, and glow details, replacing wheels with hover thrusters since no external imports are available.

For the skeleton I'm thinking chassis root, thruster joints with spinning fans, turret yaw/pitch, doors and tailgate, keeping rigging modest since this is a vehicle not a creature. For dimensions I'm going with roughly 5.5m long and 2.1m wide, and to keep the hover concept grounded I'm giving the thruster pods landing skid feet so the lowest points touch y=0 while the chassis sits around y=0.55, treating it as a landed hover-mode vehicle.

For the color palette I'm going cyberpunk dark gunmetal with neon magenta and cyan hazard stripes, planning a custom paint function with seam grids, grime, and wear rather than relying on prebuilt kit paints, using only noise, mix, smoothstep, paint, and rgb from the SDK. I'm also sketching out SVG textures I'll need, like a "HOVERWOLF" unit emblem decal and a hazard stripe pattern.

I'm planning out more SVG textures: neon tailgate text reading "ROGUE 07," a glowing HUD screen texture, a plate decal, a windscreen glass gradient with diagonal highlight streaks, a radial thruster ring glow, warning chevrons, and a glowing visor lens with scanlines.

Now I'm scoping the build itself — aiming for roughly 200-250 parts and 700-900 lines, sticking to API methods I'm confident won't throw runtime errors like box geometry, rods, sweeps, lofts, extrudes, lathes, and decals, while noting rotation conventions for orienting cylinders along different axes.

I'm setting up small geometry helper functions for boxes and cylinders, plus a wrapper to simplify creating parts with consistent bone and position options, then sketching out the body design using lofts for the main chassis and an extruded side-profile silhouette for the pickup cab shape.

Working out extrusion axes and thickness for the cab body, then planning a second narrower extrude to carve the greenhouse taper on top of the slab...

Now I'm sketching the body profile in the z-y plane, setting the chassis joint height and figuring out ground clearance so the hover pod nacelles sit correctly beneath the body at the wheel positions.

I'm making the duct open-topped with visible spinning fan blades, a glowing thrust ring at the bottom, and a floor-facing glow disc for a cyberpunk look. I'm setting up a joint hierarchy where the chassis connects to each pod via a tilt hinge, and each pod connects to its fan via a spin joint, keeping the fan's role as "hinge" for rotation.

Defining duct lathe profile...

Now I'm planning the fan assembly: seven blades plus a hub cylinder at the joint height, with a flat glowing ring underneath made from a rotated torus or thin cyan cylinder for the glow effect.

I'm now working out pod placement and strut connections, running rods and pylon boxes from the body to the pods, and checking that pod radius and position don't improperly overlap the body's underside and side skirts.

Shrinking pod radius to about 0.40-0.42 and pulling pods inward to roughly ±1.1 keeps total width around 3.0, which feels acceptable for a stylized hover design, with fender flares over the pods to tie them visually to the body.

Now I'm mapping out the side profile outline point by point, starting from the rear bottom and working forward through the bumper, hood, and up to the windscreen base to establish the vehicle's silhouette.

Finishing the lower body outline coordinates with constant wall thickness and a slight bevel, then I'll move on to defining the paint and the cab greenhouse profile separately.

I'll simplify by making the greenhouse a single tapered glass-colored extrude with dark teal gradient paint, plus body-colored roof slab and pillars, and I'm now working out the A-pillar rod geometry matching the windscreen rake angle.

For the hover conversion I'm planning four ducted pods, dual rear bell-nozzle thrusters with glow, an under-body neon strip, an anti-grav emitter plate, and a bed-mounted twin-gun turret with yaw/pitch joints alongside ammo crate, antenna, roof light bar, sensor dome, and spare battery, plus armored door plates with hazard stripes.

Now I'm adding ERA bricks on the hood, a front ram bumper with glowing slit headlights, vented grille, fender smoke launchers, and a bull bar instead of a winch, along with magenta underglow and cyan edge accents and a hot pink kanji decal on the door. For decals I'm placing flat plane parts with textures positioned just outside the body's side faces, oriented to face outward on each door.

I'm working out the plane orientation math so text on the side decals reads correctly when viewed from either side of the car, calculating the local axes for each facing direction to make sure the text isn't mirrored.

Now I'm moving on to planning out the specific coordinates for each vehicle part.

Doors need separate overlay geometry from the body shell: a thin panel box positioned at the cab's side faces, including handle, armor plate, emblem, and mirror details, hinged at the door's front-top edge. I'm also placing a tailgate hinge joint at the rear of the bed.

Now I'm laying out the truck bed walls and pedestal dimensions, then placing the turret's yaw joint near the top of the pedestal and a pitch joint slightly above and forward of it to allow the gun barrel to elevate.

I'm checking whether the barrels would clip through the cab roof when pointed forward at low elevation, since the cab spans higher than the pedestal mount — this means I'd need either a taller pedestal to clear the roofline or a different firing angle, though a very tall pintle mount starts to look impractical for a technical-style vehicle.

Instead I'm reconsidering the layout entirely: putting a remote weapon station with twin autocannon on the roof itself (centered, pitch joint raised above windscreen height so the barrels clear forward), and using the bed for a tilted missile pod rack plus a generator/battery pack. Checking the geometry, a 35° upward tilt on the bed launcher still clips the cab roof at typical bed-to-cab distances, so that angle won't clear either.

Switching to a vertical launch system in the bed instead—a 2x3 grid of hex missile cells with hatch lids, one hatch open showing a glowing pink interior—avoids clearance problems entirely and looks better. For the roof I'm finalizing the RWS turret with yaw ring, pitch cradle, twin barrels with muzzle brakes, ammo box, and a glowing sensor eye, plus a front light bar, rear antenna array, and dome sensor. At the rear I'm planning the tailgate with a neon sign above twin main thruster bell nozzles mounted below the bed deck, angled to point backward.

I'm sizing the thruster nozzle profile, checking it doesn't overlap the floor slab and adjusting length down to about 0.45m so the total vehicle length stays near 6 meters. Now I'm designing the front bumper with angled ram plates and tooth spikes, plus slim neon strip headlights glowing cyan-white under a brow for the cyberpunk look.

I'm working out the front grille with dark horizontal vents and a center emblem, then shaping the hood with a sloped surface formula, a raised central ridge, staggered ERA bricks along the sides, and vent details positioned relative to that slope.

Now I'm calculating the hood tilt angle at about 6.2 degrees and applying a positive rotation about the X axis so the hood surface pitches forward correctly, before moving on to the wheel-arch flares over the outboard pods.

I'm working out the pylon pod mounts — plates connecting the body sill out to each pod, with a rod linking the pod collar up to the chassis attachment point, defining their positions and radius.

Then I'm adding diagonal braces front and back for the pods, plus magenta glow strips along the underside sills, and starting work on a central gravity core cylinder with emitter elements underneath the body.

Now I'm placing side skirt armor plates and checking they don't clash with the pod positions along the z-axis, then moving on to the cab doors and window openings.

Next I'm adding greenhouse glass, door armor slats, and camera-pod mirrors with glowing lenses, then planning the bed interior with ribbed walls, equipment racks, and glowing battery cells connected by cables, possibly routed up to the turret. Finally I'm sketching the roof rack lighting, a radar unit, and exterior decals like license plates and hazard stripes on the ram bumper.

For colors, I'm settling on a cyberpunk-military palette: deep indigo hull, gunmetal-navy body panels, olive-grey armor plating, and magenta neon accents for contrast against the darker tones.

Writing hull paint function...

Still defining paint variants for armor, metal, and rubber, plus a glow helper for flat-colored parts. I'm sketching the texture assets next: a hexagonal wolf emblem badge for the door reading "HX-9," and a neon tail sign with glowing cyan text like "NIGHT RUNNER" on a dark background.

I'm also planning hazard chevron stripes for the skirts and rear bumper, a glowing HUD display panel on the cab's rear wall with readouts like "AMMO 24/24 BAT 87%," and a slit-shaped lens texture with a glow gradient for headlights or visor details.

I'm designing a radial-gradient swirl texture for the thruster ring, visible only from below the pod, plus a windscreen plane with a dark teal gradient, light streak, and tiny HUD overlay since the extruded greenhouse geometry can't take textures directly.

Working out the windscreen plane's exact position, taper, and tilt to match the fuselage's narrowing tumblehome and compute its correct surface normal...

For the side windows, I need the same tapering logic, with the glass plane normal tilting slightly upward to follow the inward slope from a thicker base to a narrower top.

I'll skip adding dedicated side glass planes since the body paint already reads as glass with a diagonal streak, but I'll keep a windscreen texture with faint wiper lines and a subtle cyan HUD-style corner detail since it's cheap and adds character. Moving on to the license plate texture next.

For remaining details, I'm settling on a plate reading "H0V-3R 2077," an ammo crate stencil with yellow "AP-HEAT ▲" text, and skipping the tally-mark kill counter idea for simplicity -- bringing the texture set to nine total: EMBLEM, SIGN, HAZARD, HUD, SLIT, THRUST, GLASS, PLATE, STENCIL. I need to make sure each SVG has a proper viewBox, uses safe monospace/sans-serif fonts, and keeps stroke widths thick enough to render clearly at the target raster size.

I'm also deciding against adding dangling cards like streamers or exhaust wash effects since the lighting risk outweighs the payoff, so I'll skip those and keep the part construction focused on textured planes with proper material mapping for glow effects.

Still, I'll add rear thrust plumes as crossed cards anchored to the chassis bone, using layered teardrop-shaped flame textures with alpha cutoff for sharp edges rather than soft gradient fades.

Now I'm setting up the module imports from the builder SDK, pulling in the geometry and texture helpers along with the glow kit, and confirming the exported functions cover everything needed for the build.

I'm starting the build function by creating the main spine joint, then defining a small helper function that attaches part geometry, color, and position relative to that root joint for convenience.

I'll define a local type alias for the options parameter to keep things reasonably typed without over-engineering, since strict enforcement likely isn't critical here. Confirming `rotation` and other options like `flat` and `texture` are valid for `b.part`, then starting to write out the actual sections.

Setting up geometry helper functions for boxes, cylinders, and cones, plus building out a color palette with hull, armor, and dark tones, and a procedural steel paint using noise and smoothstep for a metallic streak effect.

I'm defining the rest of the color palette with magenta, cyan, yellow, rubber, glass, and orange accents, keeping it small since each color counts toward a shader limit. Now I'm sketching the overall build order: skeleton components like chassis, pods, doors, tailgate, turret, and VLS hatch, followed by body shell extrusions, doors, bed, pods and struts, rear thrusters, and roof geometry.

Setting up thruster pods and fan joints...

Checking that the outline's winding and the bevel operation can handle a nine-vertex shape with a concave corner -- it should just shrink the bevel until it fits. The resulting lower body slab spans a fairly wide range from y 0.55 to 1.34, so it's a sizable box underlying the hood region.

Now I'm sketching the cab greenhouse, extruding a four-point outline along the z-axis with a thickness that tapers from the lowest to highest point, using the glass color. For the roof, I'm placing a box slightly wider than the glass top to create an overhang, positioning it to cover the depth of the cabin.

Then I'm working out the pillars: A-pillars as rods running diagonally from the beltline up to the roof corners with a hexagonal cross-section, and considering how to handle the C-pillars as wider rear slabs or similar rod connections for the B-pillar line.

For the rear window, I'm deciding whether the sloped rear face should be glass or armored plating, since I'd originally wanted a HUD panel there but that conflicts with a transparent rear window—so I'm thinking about making it a solid raked panel instead and working out its tilt angle from the geometry.

Working out armor box orientation using a direction/axis convention, then computing the rear panel and HUD plane positions along the sloped line.

Now I'm figuring out the windscreen's placement and tilt, computing its offset and size based on the hull's taper, and positioning the A-pillar rods relative to the glass edges.

I'm sketching small details like wiper boxes on the windscreen, then moving to the front fascia: a dark grille box with horizontal slat rods and a possible magenta glow strip behind them for depth.

Now I'm designing the headlights as slit-lamp housings with a glowing cyan slit, a brow piece above, and a lower fog lamp, then starting the front bumper with an angled ram plate shape.

Adding underside spikes using a spike helper function with direction and radius params, skipping a roo bar/push bar addition, and starting the hood with a tilted center ridge box near the hood's front.

Now I'm detailing the hood add-ons: glowing cyan vent slits behind slat bars, ERA armor tiles arranged as 2x3 brick grids on each hood slope (12 pieces total), and smoke launcher mounts near the front fenders.

Still positioning parts...

Now I'm setting up the doors: a hinge joint on each side of the chassis for the door swing, plus the door panel itself as a box bone colored with the hull material, sized and positioned to span the side opening.

Working out the lamellar armor plate layering on the door, tilting each strip's rotation so the top edge angles outward away from the body for a layered plated look.

I'm also figuring out the handle placement and resolving the conflict between the emblem decal and the armor plates by consolidating the door armor into a single beveled plate so the emblem has clean space to sit on.

I'm placing the door bolts, a hazard stripe, and working out the mirror assembly—stalk rod, dark pod housing, and a small glowing lens—mounted near the A-pillar.

Now I'm positioning side skirts to clear the wheel pods front and rear, adding a hazard texture strip and a magenta glow strip underneath for accent lighting.

I'm trying a sponson flare over the pods but realize it would block the fan opening visible from above, so I'm scrapping that idea and keeping just the pod struts exposed instead.

Now I'm working out the strut geometry connecting the pod rim to the body: two rods per pod positioned fore and aft of the rim, plus a mounting block near the skirt to anchor them to the body's half-width.

I'm also adding a fan guard over each pod—a flat torus ring across the top with thin cross rods for safety spokes—and detailing the bottom with a glowing thrust-plume disc facing downward, plus an outer glow ring around the duct's lower rim.

Now I'm building the fan mechanism: a steel hub cylinder mounted on the fan bone, surrounded by eight blade boxes positioned radially outward, each rotated with both a yaw angle around the hub and a pitch tilt to give the blades proper airfoil angle.

Now I'm defining the duct lathe geometry attached to the pod joint, then adding an inner glow ring near the top lip for a subtle highlight. I'm also considering small rib boxes around the outer wall as heat fins, arranged in an angled ring across the pods.

Shifting to the bed section, I'm laying out the floor extrude with dark rib boxes, then sizing the side walls as boxes positioned relative to the tailgate at the rear, working out their z-span and height against the deck. I'm also adding a rail cap box along the top edge in armor material.

Continuing, I'm placing vertical rib boxes along the sides, a headboard panel box at the front in armor material, and a tailgate joint with its hinge panel in hull material plus a rear-facing sign plane, where I'm working out the local axis orientation for that plane given its backward-facing direction.

I'm adding a neon trim strip along the tailgate's top edge, then positioning the rear bumper/hitch box and reconciling it with the rear thruster nozzle placement so the tailgate panel, nozzle mouths, and floor slab don't overlap in vertical space.

Still shaping the lathe profile points...

Now I'm positioning the mouth glow disc and exhaust plume geometry near the jet's rear, then moving on to the VLS cell box dimensions for the ship's interior bed layout.

I'm laying out the six hex hatches in a 3x2 grid atop the VLS box, figuring their x/z spacing so they fit within the box footprint, and deciding one hatch should be posed open via a hinge joint while the rest stay closed in the rest pose.

Working out the rotation direction for the open hatch lid, I settle on a -65 degree tilt about the X hinge axis so the forward edge lifts upward correctly, then plan to add a glowing magenta interior visible beneath the open lid.

I'm adding a small missile element inside the open cell—a short cylinder body with a cone nose tip, colored metallic gray with a magenta tip accent—and noting that the pose rotation needs to happen after all the lid's child parts are built, since posing carries everything attached to that joint along with it.

Next I'm planning the battery cells for the rear bed: two vertical cylinders with glowing cyan ring bands, connected by drooping cable sweeps to a nearby VLS point, plus an ammo crate box with a stencil marking on its side.

Rotating that cylinder to lie along Z for the coolant tank. For the bed, I'm thinking about adding a rollbar arch made from a swept rod shape over the back, though I need to check it doesn't clash with the cab roof's rear position.

For the roof, I'm adding a light bar housing with glow strips in cyan and magenta, plus a dome sensor built as a glass hemisphere with a ring base and small cyan glow on the rear roof.

Now I'm placing the antenna array with a mast, crossbars, and a tapering whip antenna with a glowing red/magenta tip, then working out smoke launcher positions and resolving a layout conflict between the RWS turret ring and the dome sensor placement.

I'm now building out the turret mechanism itself — yaw and pitch joints, a flat base ring, a drum on the yaw axis, the yaw box and cheek plates, the pitch cradle, and twin barrel rods extending forward.

Then I'm adding shrouds around the barrels, muzzle brakes with side ports, outboard ammo boxes, and a sensor assembly up front with a glowing lens and a small camera box. I'm also checking barrel length against the vehicle's windscreen to avoid clipping.

For the underbody, I'm placing a dark sled box as the gravity core base plus a thin glowing plane just beneath it to create a magenta underglow effect visible from low side angles, giving the hover-car a lit gap above the ground.

I'm splitting the glow into cyan emitter discs centered underneath and a magenta border strip around the edges, plus adjusting the duct lathe geometry so its bottom sits exactly at ground level for proper contact. Overall height checks out fine with the antenna whip reaching about 3.2 units and the turret barrel around 2.5.

I'll shorten the whip antenna slightly to 0.9, and confirm the x-extent stays within roughly ±1.55 once mirrors and pod edges are factored in. Now I'm writing diagonal hazard-stripe paint logic for the ram plate surface and starting a glass material paint function...

Still writing glass paint and hull paint helper...

Still writing panel seam logic...

Good, the door panels align with the stripe coordinates so it reads as continuous across the body. I'm also defining an armor paint variant and a steel paint, keeping glow parts flat-colored, then moving on to drafting SVG textures for an emblem design using layered polygons with dark fill and magenta stroke outlines.

Writing emblem SVG...

Designing more HUD-style icons...

Writing plume teardrop path...

For the plume texture, I'm shaping a teardrop that's wide at the bottom (rooted at the nozzle) and narrows toward the tip, layered in magenta, cyan, and white for depth. With all nine textures plus the reused hazard pattern done, I'm now thinking through decal plane sizing and making sure dark-background textures don't trigger unwanted glow.

I'm deciding which parts should glow: sign, HUD, slit, and thrust elements get emissive glow while glass, hazard, and stencil-style textures stay flat. Now I'm writing helper functions for placing parts and texture-mapped planes on the chassis bone, making sure option overrides spread correctly so bone and direction settings can be customized per call.

Writing build function and types...

Defining chassis joints and pod positions...

Adding fins and struts around the duct...

I'm realizing the pod and body nearly touch with barely any gap, which hides most of the fan opening since only the portion with x>0.95 is actually visible past the body — so I should shift the pod outward to get better visibility.

Working through the pod geometry at x=1.2, I'm checking the duct opening against the body edge and skirt boundary to confirm it's mostly exposed, then sketching the outrigger-style struts connecting the body underside to the pod collar.

Placing the strut beams outside the duct's rim radius so they clear the opening, offsetting them in z by ±0.4 at x≈0.95 to avoid intersecting the duct top.

Now I'm adding the fan guard: a thin glowing cyan torus hugging the inner lip for visual accent, plus two crossing rods spanning the opening to suggest a protective grille.

Checking that the lowest geometry — the duct base and ring — sits right at floor level so nothing clips below ground, then tallying up the rough part count across pods, body, doors, bed, roof, and other sections to gauge overall complexity, landing somewhere around 300+ parts total.

Setting up the module imports and type usage for the builder, then defining the meta block with the component name and description, and planning to keep texture setup as top-level constants before moving into the hull paint definitions.

Now I'm building out the main `build()` function, setting up helper functions for parts, planes with textures, and rods, all bound to the chassis joint with sensible defaults...

Writing body geometry...

Positioning the roof slab just above the glass top so they meet cleanly, then placing three pairs of rod pillars connecting the hull's lower edge to the roof edge at different widths, checking that each pillar sits roughly aligned with the glass taper from bottom to top.

I'm sketching smaller trim pieces now -- a thin sill box along the side, considering a neon beltline glow strip but deciding to skip it since the magenta paint stripe already covers that area, then moving to the windscreen wipers as two thin black boxes positioned and angled along the base of the windscreen glass.

Next I'm adding a cyan glow strip across the top edge of the nose/hood as a small accent light.

Now I'm designing the front grille: a dark backing box with horizontal steel slats, a magenta backlight glow panel positioned just behind the slats, and a center vertical bar to anchor the composition.

For the emblem, I'm placing a small hexagonal glowing cylinder centered on the bar. I need to figure out where to put the license plate too -- the front bumper location conflicts with the Ram-style plate, so I'm moving it instead to the rear, mounting it on the body slab beneath the tailgate.

Checking the rear plate against the thruster mount plates at ±0.55, I narrow the plate to 0.36x0.12 so it clears the mounts, positioning it just under the tailgate. For the headlights, I'm placing housing boxes near the front fascia corners at x ±0.7 with a slit plane slightly in front for the lens glow, making sure the facing direction is correct.

I'm skipping the brow and fog lamp details since they conflict with existing plate geometry, and settling on a bumper layout with a center hazard-colored plate and side armor plates angled slightly outward, while starting to plan the underbelly spikes.

Still placing spikes and bolts...

Still placing parts... now working out the hazard stripe plane on the skirt, then moving to rearview mirrors, bed walls with hull paint, and the tailgate panel joint positioning.

Finishing the plume glow cards, then double-checking that glow works correctly with cards' per-texture materials and doesn't accidentally trip the paint-color safeguard.

Now I'm placing the lathed thrusters, building out the VLS and roll hoop sweep, then positioning floodlight pods angled back near the top of the hoop.

Adding glow lens and cable sweeps...

Now I'm laying out the VLS hatch grid with small cylindrical lids and glow indicator dots, positioning one hatch open with a hinge at the back edge to show an armed launch tube.

Checking the hinge rotation math confirms the lid swings upward correctly with the -70° pose. For the RWS I'll leave the pitch joint neutral, and I'm thinking about adding militarized touches like roof light bar details and a big "07" roof decal number for identification.

Now I need to work out the orientation of that roof marking texture so the text reads correctly from above, with the front of the drawing facing the vehicle's front and figuring out which local axis corresponds to the model's right side.

Deciding to skip a dedicated roof or hood emblem since the ring and ridge geometry there would conflict, and moving on to compile the final texts into SVG markup.

Writing HUD SVG code...

The SVG battery indicator looks good now. I'm verifying the hull noise function and extrude options, confirming the taper array and color paint parameters are correctly specified before finalizing.

Now I'm defining the turret joints with yaw and pitch hinges, then placing the torus, cylinder arm, and box geometry pieces for the chassis mount at their respective positions...

Still writing barrel geometry...

Smoke launcher tubes get placed with angled rods and caps, then I'm adding an antenna mast with crossbar and whip, plus a dome detail. I'll skip neon kanji signage due to font issues, and move on to underbody details like the sled, discs, and a simple anti-grav core ring.

I verify the pod mounting positions align with the beam spans, double-check the torus rotation to confirm its normal faces correctly, and confirm the fan joint parenting works before thinking through rest pose rules for the creature.

Now I'm moving to final assembly, counting textures and paints for consistency. I'm writing the paint logic that assigns magenta or hull colors to the body based on surface normal and position, handling the hood slope and door panel ranges as special cases.

Still deciding where hazard striping goes — skipping the rear bumper due to mount plate conflicts, settling on hazard texture for skirts and the ram plate paint instead. Now I'm writing out the final part.

For the glass, I'm setting up the windscreen as an extruded plane using the glass paint and tint value. Then I need to check that I'm only importing what's actually used to avoid unused-import typecheck errors — keeping createBuilder, frame, mix, noise, paint, smoothstep, svg, polyline, catmull, and the Fill/Joint types since each is referenced somewhere, like catmull for the cables and polyline for the roll hoop.

Setting up the hull paint instance and starting the SVG builder...

Writing hazard stripe SVG...

Now I'm adding the door joints for each side, computing a left/right suffix and attaching a hinge joint to the chassis at a mirrored x-position, then continuing with the mirror attachment points.

Placing the ERA bricks along the hood surface...

Adding the hood ridge box with a cyan glow strip, computing hoodY for the cab, and planning the VLS frame ring and body color before wrapping up with the final return statement.

Now I'm repositioning the VLS launcher further back to avoid overlap with the headboard, adjusting its depth and hatch placements, plus setting coordinates for the hinge, batteries, and crate relative to the new VLS center.

Checking battery-crate overlap at the back, I shift batteries deeper along z to clear the crate while keeping clearance from the tailgate, then trim the coolant tank's length so it doesn't intrude into the VLS footprint.

For the hazard decal, I decide it makes more sense placed on the rear-facing face of the VLS where it'll actually be visible, since the headboard gap is too small to matter.

Now I'm writing the steel sweep geometry code for connecting elements...

With the TS types close enough to acceptable, I'm ready to write out the full file, expecting it'll land around 600 lines.
